canberra.title: ‘I started to feel invisible’: Canberra artist Liz Lea turns women’s midlife stories into a celebration of ageing
canberra.snippet: When internationally acclaimed Canberra dancer and choreographer Liz Lea turned 40, she began to feel invisible. Work became harder to fi...
canberra.content:
Liz Lea performs in Diamond, a one-woman production exploring ageing, menopause and resilience through dance, song and cabaret. Photo: O&J Wikner Photography.

When internationally acclaimed Canberra dancer and choreographer Liz Lea turned 40, she began to feel invisible.

Work became harder to find. She questioned where she belonged. Then came menopause.

“I just thought I was going a bit nuts,” she says.

For years, Lea believed she was navigating those changes alone. She wasn’t.

While developing her new one-woman production Diamond, Lea invited women from Canberra and Queanbeyan to share their experiences of ageing, menopause and midlife. Instead of hearing dozens of different stories, she found herself hearing the same one over and over.

“They all thought it was just them.”

Women spoke about brain fog, sleepless nights, changing careers, shifting identities and trying to understand bodies that suddenly felt unfamiliar. Many had spent years believing they were the only ones experiencing it.

Those conversations transformed Diamond from a deeply personal work into a shared story about resilience, reinvention and the often-overlooked experiences of ageing women.

The production follows RED, Lea’s acclaimed autobiographical solo work inspired by living with endometriosis for 35 years — a condition that ultimately meant she could not have children. If RED explored loss, Diamond looks at what comes next.

Lea says one of the biggest surprises was discovering how little women knew about menopause before experiencing it.

“We’re trying to navigate work, families and everyday life while wondering what on earth is going on,” she says.

Diamond evolved from a deeply personal work into a shared story about resilience and reinvention. Photo: O&J Wikner Photography.

Among all the women she met, one conversation has stayed with her.

A 75-year-old woman told Lea she loved becoming invisible.

Rather than seeing ageing as something to fear, she described it as freedom — freedom from expectations and from constantly worrying about how others saw her.

“She’s able to live her life on her terms,” Lea says.

“I found that really empowering.”

The conversation also made Lea rethink her own experience.

Although she remembers feeling overlooked in her 40s, she says her career has since flourished. More importantly, she realised ageing wasn’t simply about what women lose.

“It’s definitely about how we redefine ourselves as we get older, how we see ourselves and how we are valued.”

That idea sits at the heart of Diamond.

Despite tackling subjects often discussed in whispers, Lea says audiences should not expect a sombre evening.

“It’s not a downer,” she laughs. “It’s basically a musical comedy.”

Humour, music and dance sit alongside honest conversations about menopause, friendship, identity and the freedom many women discover as they grow older.

Lea also hopes the show resonates with men.

Three male community performers are part of the production, reflecting her belief that menopause and ageing are conversations families and partners should have together.

“We don’t go through these experiences alone,” she says.

“We need the support of the people around us.”

She hopes the show gives audiences a better understanding of what many women experience, often silently.

An ACT Artist of the Year and Australian Dance Award recipient, Lea has spent more than three decades creating work across Australia, Europe, Asia, Africa and the United States.

Diamond is the second work in a trilogy that began with RED, drawing on both her own experiences and the stories of local women to start conversations that are often left until much later in life.

Presented as part of Q the Locals, Diamond will have its world premiere at The Q, Queanbeyan Performing Arts Centre, on 6 and 7 August at 7:30 pm, and 8 August at 2 pm and 7:30 pm.

canberra.title: WATCH: Young pianists strike a chord with a public piano recital (and half a million views)
canberra.snippet: A video of young performers playing a public piano at Westfield Woden has attracted over 500,000 views online. It has sparked the questio...
canberra.content:
A video of two boys playing a local piano at Westfield Woden has gone viral, amassing over 550,000 views on social media. Photo: Holly Winchester.

A video of young performers playing a public piano at Westfield Woden has attracted over 500,000 views online. It has sparked the question: should there be more public instruments available around Canberra?

Holly Winchester, who recorded the video, said she was overjoyed to be sitting next to the piano when the two boys started playing a classical piece.

She admitted that while she normally expects teenagers in malls to cause a commotion, she was blown away by the talent of the person playing.

“There were two young boys at Woden tonight, not on e-bikes or scooters, not causing trouble, but sitting at the public piano, filling the mall with beautiful music,” she said.

“Thank you both for letting me film and share your talent.

“You were an absolute joy to listen to, and your parents should be incredibly proud. Sometimes just a simple moment can restore your faith in the next generation.”

Her video of the pair went viral, attracting over 550,000 views on Facebook alone, receiving over 14,000 likes.

Others shared Holly’s opinion of the public piano, with many believing instruments like the one at Westfield Woden should be more common places.

“I see kiddos on here frequently — there are tonnes of wonderful teens out there, and the majority of them are beautiful humans just wanting connection,” said regular Woden shopper Jessica McEwan.

“Thanks for sharing the moment. I’ve never seen that piano played well before. I hope more people use it to practice,” Ginger Rogers said.

Westfield Woden responded to the video’s virality, stating that it is proud to offer a resource that people can play and enjoy.

“We’re always looking for ways to create spaces where people can connect and spend time together at Westfield Woden, and it’s been great to see customers enjoying our piano and making it part of their visit,” Westfield Woden Centre Manager Craig Smellie said.

“The positive response to this video is nice to see and highlights the value of shared community spaces. Something as simple as a musical instrument can enhance the customer experience and encourage meaningful connections in our community.”

According to Pianos Pub, there are currently 15 public pianos across the ACT, with seven located in the CBD and one each in Lyneham, Belconnen, Dickson, Gungahlin, Woden, Stromlo, Tuggeranong and Capital Hill.

canberra.title: Hospitality from the heart at Braidwood’s Casanova’s
canberra.snippet: It takes immense skill and restraint to make complexity look simple, and no one does it better than Casanova’s, a cafe and bakery located...
canberra.content:
The Scandi-esque fit-out at Casanova’s is thoughtful and welcoming. Photo: Tenele Conway.

It takes immense skill and restraint to make complexity look simple, and no one does it better than Casanova’s, a cafe and bakery located in the heritage town of Braidwood.

Tucked away just behind the shops of Wallace Street on the well-worn Canberra-to-Coast trail, it’s the sort of place that has a word-of-mouth following that over the years has become a little cult-like.

You don’t have to look far for proof of their reputation. Shopkeepers instinctively point hungry visitors towards Casanova’s, and both Canberrans and coast-dwellers swap stories of the sourdough they never miss picking up on the drive through. It has an intangible draw that will see you come back time and again and have you telling everyone about it.

Inside their heritage doors you’ll find a thoughtful and welcoming space.

The original ceiling beams have been removed to make way for a vaulted ceiling. Half-curtained windows let in the long afternoon light. The polished concrete floors bring industrial chic to the otherwise timber fit-out, and the unkillable houseplant pothos dotted on the shelves scream a love of greenery paired with a tentative commitment to maintaining indoor plant life, a trick that more cafes should take note of.

Casanova’s has built quite the reputation for their seasonal menu and fresh-baked goods. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Alongside the Scandi-esque fit-out, there’s a display of like-minded cookbooks focusing on simplicity, a cabinet filled with tempting golden pastries and a 70s soundtrack best summed up as uplifting nostalgia that all accumulates into a clear ethos of effortless perfection.

Sitting down to a bowl of broccoli soup on my recent visit, I was swept up in Casanova’s carefully crafted experience, and before I lose you at broccoli, let me tell you why you should keep reading.

Broccoli isn’t really my thing; it conjures soggy textures of times gone by that I’d rather forget. Yet the team at Casanova’s, headed up by owners Joe Lawrence and Jacqui Casanova, know a thing or two about broccoli.

The first thing is that it’s seasonal and should be served at its best during our wonderfully chilly winters.

Second, nobody, especially not Casanova’s, puts broccoli in the corner; it’s the hero of the dish here, and the accompanying flavours of gorgonzola, which is mixed through the soup itself, and the house-made sourdough are there to play their part in what they know is a broccoli party.

The broccoli soup heroes the winter veg and takes the flavours up a level with gorgonzola and crusty sourdough. Photo: Tenele Conway.

If you’re still not convinced, shall we talk cauliflower? Or maybe pumpkin, lentils or hazelnuts are your thing? If any of those strike a chord, you’re in luck; they all appear on the current winter menu, which comes together as a real celebration of the season.

There’s a reason that produce is so respected at Casanova’s, and that’s because they grow much of it themselves, an undertaking that fits with their philosophy of doing as much as possible from scratch.

If you’re still hesitant on the winter vegetable front, there is a sourdough pizza menu made on gorgeously puffy handmade sourdough bases. The current flavours lean into rich Italian meats with tomato-based prosciutto and salami pizzas, or you can go vegetarian with the spinach, mozzarella, feta, preserved lemon, ricotta and pine nuts.

Sipping my brewed chai with a belly full of broccoli, singing emanates from the open kitchen as a staff member harmonises to Fleetwood Mac. It’s one of those little moments that reminds you the best hospitality can’t be manufactured; it has to be genuine and from the heart, and that’s what Casanova’s has in spades.

Casanova’s is located at 68 Wallace Street, Braidwood. They’re open Monday until Saturday from 8 am until 2 pm and for dinner on Fridays from 5 pm until 8 pm.

canberra.title: Back when steam propelled the first horseless carriage through the region
canberra.snippet: On the Friday afternoon of 4 May 1900, residents of Wagga Wagga were treated to the extraordinary sights and sounds of a horseless carria...
canberra.content:
Thompson’s Motor Phaeton was the first self-propelled road vehicle seen in the Riverina. Photo: Museums Victoria.

On the Friday afternoon of 4 May 1900, residents of Wagga Wagga were treated to the extraordinary sights and sounds of a horseless carriage clattering its way across the dusty, rutted surface of Fitzmaurice Street.

“No small amount of interest was created in town yesterday afternoon, by the arrival of a motor car, the first which has made its appearance in Wagga,” wrote the Wagga Wagga Express.

“The vehicle was a ‘Thompson’ make, and was in charge of the inventor Mr H Thompson, and Mr S L Holmes.”

Through the middle of the 19th century steam power had steadily transformed Australia’s waterways and the expanding railway networks had linked the far-flung cities and regions. But at the turn of the century the roads remained little more than dusty tracks ruled by horse-drawn vehicles and bullock drays.

As inventors across the globe tinkered with the idea of self-propelled road vehicles, Melbourne cousins Herbert Thompson and Edward Holmes were determined to demonstrate that the motor car was the way of the future down under.

Herbert constructed his first steam engine at 19 for use in a launch on the Yarra River and, after training as an engineer, he set himself up as a manufacturer of steam engines and boilers in the Melbourne suburb of Armadale. He and Edward built their steam-powered ‘Motor Phaeton’ in 1896 and had it fully operational by July 1899.

It was described as “quiet and smooth-running” and the six-seat carriage was made of fiddle-back ash and silky oak. It had a kerosene fuelled, two-cylinder engine and was proving to be a hit during exhibitions at sporting grounds and public events.

The wooden bodied steam car created by Herbert Thomson completed a 794 km trip from Bathurst to Melbourne in April / May 1900. Museums Victoria.

The phaeton caused a stir on the nation’s biggest stage at the 1900 Easter Show in Sydney where locals debated the safety of introducing such an unwieldly looking contraption to the city’s busy streets.

The cousins deftly demonstrated their ability to control the motorised marvel and announced their intention for a record setting interstate drive from the Central West to Melbourne via the Riverina.

“The Thompson car, the production of a Melbourne engineer, is propelled by steam, and is built as a phaeton fitted with Dunlop pneumatic carriage tires, the whole forming a compact and handsome turnout,” recorded the Queenslander newspaper.

“It is the intention of the builder and designer to attempt an overland trip with his car from Sydney to Melbourne, 604 miles, a route that is hilly and rough enough to test the strength and endurance of a bullock-waggon, let alone a light phaeton.”

In late April, Herbert and Edward loaded the phaeton with water and kerosene and set off from Bathurst at an average speed of 14 km/h. Herbert explained that he wanted to “err on the side of safety”, however on one downhill section of the journey they reached hair-raising speeds of 24 km/h and managed to outpace a pair of horses over a 19 km stretch.

The journey was far from straightforward with inevitable mechanical breakdowns and frequent stops for repairs and to replenish water supplies for the thirsty steam boiler. It also had only one forward gear, meaning that the belt needed to be manually shortened before a climb.

Steep, rocky hills tested the vehicle’s capabilities, while boggy sections and river crossings often required ingenuity and the occasional assistance of a passing bullock dray or horse-drawn wagon.

The Cootamundra Herald described the excitement as the never-before-seen spectacle rolled through town.

“As it glided through the streets, heads were bobbing at every door. But a quarter of an hour and the interesting piece of mechanism was on the road once more, en route to Buthungra, leaving knots of curious people collected wherever it had halted,” they wrote.

“A cyclist accompanied them a few miles along the road to view the action of the machine upon the hills, and he came back to report that it ‘took the three’ of them all their time, with full steam on, to push the heavy vehicle up the gap hill.

“Doubtless this weakness will in time be overcome, and then the old horse will have to stand aside.”

According to the Wagga Wagga Express, the 70 km journey from Bethungra to Wagga was covered in 2 hours 20 minutes and included a “slight mishap” at Junee where Herbert swerved to avoid a rut and damaged a tyre.

In the end, the marathon run from Bathurst to Melbourne was completed in just five days and stands as an important milestone in Australian motoring history, marking the beginning of the country’s transition to the automobile.

Original Article published by Chris Roe on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: After 24 years, Ngunnawal Bush Healing Farm begins journey to community control
canberra.snippet: More than two decades after Ngunnawal Elders first called for a culturally grounded healing place on Country, the ACT Government has begu...
canberra.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith and Ngunnawal elder Aunty Violet Sheridan.

More than two decades after Ngunnawal Elders first called for a culturally grounded healing place on Country, the ACT Government has begun the process of transitioning the Ngunnawal Bush Healing Farm to Aboriginal community control.

The Government announced on 29 July that it would work with Aboriginal organisation Yeddung Mura to oversee the transition, describing it as a major milestone in a project first envisioned by the community in 2002.

The Healing Farm was conceived as a residential healing facility where Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people could strengthen their connection to culture, family and Country while receiving support for issues including alcohol and other drug dependence.

Although the ACT Government purchased the Miowera property in 2008 and established a day program, the original vision of a community-controlled residential healing service has never been realised.

Health Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said the transition marked an important step in fulfilling that long-held ambition.

“It’s always been the government’s intention to transition to a residential service under community control,” she said.

“There’s still a lot of water to go under the bridge before it’s a community-controlled residential service, but this decision is a really important milestone.”

The ACT Government will continue operating the current day program while working with Yeddung Mura to develop the pathway towards community control. No timeframe has been announced for completing the transition.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Minister Suzanne Orr said the move would help deliver the original vision for the site.

“With the right support and resourcing, this transition provides an opportunity to realise the original vision – comprehensive, wraparound and Community-led healing that responds to the needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the ACT and surrounding regions,” she said.

The announcement comes as Aboriginal community control of culturally significant sites gains momentum in the ACT. Last week, the government established an interim joint community-government management committee to oversee the transition of Boomanulla Oval back to Aboriginal community control under the ACT Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Agreement 2019–2028.

The Healing Farm supports some of the ACT’s most vulnerable Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people through its existing day program. The government said transitioning the service to community control recognised that healing was most effective when it was led by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and shaped by community.

Indigenous Australians continue to experience disproportionately higher rates of alcohol and other drug-related harm than the broader population, with young Aboriginal Australians around five times more likely to be hospitalised or die from an alcohol or other drug-related condition.

Region contacted the ACT Government’s Office for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs (OATSIA) and Aunty Roslyn Brown for comment. A response was not received before publication.

australia.title: First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds
australia.snippet: Helicopter surveillance finds dead and dying greater crested terns off South Australian coast as H5 virus spreads Get our breaking news e...
australia.content:
More than 80 dead and sick birds seen on rocks off the South Australian coast are suspected to be the first mass mortality event from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, only six weeks after the disease arrived in Australia.

Authorities reported on Saturday that helicopter surveillance had revealed 49 dead greater crested terns on Baudin Rocks, near Robe, as well as 35 more sick terns.

While some of the birds had been collected for testing, South Australia’s chief vet Skye Freuan said it was likely the first mass mortality event from the disease.

South Australia also reported three suspected positive cases in other greater crested terns, including one inland at Monarto, suggesting the disease has begun moving away from the coast. The Monarto area is home to several poultry farms.

Three silver gulls were also suspected positive, SA authorities said, adding to the first silver gull found a few days ago and confirmed positive by the CSIRO earlier on Saturday.

Kate Millar, the chief executive of conservation charity BirdLife Australia, called it a “very significant escalation of the bird flu situation in Australia, and a very bleak milestone”.

“Sadly, we’re at the beginning of a long and challenging battle and birds and wildlife are going to need all the help they can get,” she said.

Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said it now appeared the disease was “starting to take off” and “mirroring the experience in South America of early detections, then rapid increases in numbers and spread leading to mass mortality events in wildlife.”

“We are still at the very early stages of this devastating disease spreading, but the possible first mass mortality coming just days after the virus was declared not eradicable indicates how quickly this could escalate,” he said.

Freuan said there was “nothing we can do” to stop the spread of the disease, but that surveillance was working.

The news came at the end of a significant week in the development of the disease when numbers jumped by 20 in just a few days to the current total of 53.

Australia was the last continent to have the unwelcome arrival of a disease that has killed millions of birds and mammals around the world.

Victoria this week confirmed its first cases of the virulent strain in a greater crested tern found in Portland, with the state joining Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland that have all recorded positive cases.

On Saturday, Victorian authorities said samples from five crested terns had been sent to the CSIRO laboratory in Geelong, with preliminary testing suggesting more positive results.

Five confirmed cases in birds at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island also raised concerns for the welfare of the area’s Australian sea lions – an endangered species. Tens of thousands of seals have died worldwide from the disease.

But it has been the cases among silver gulls that has experts like Sean Dooley, the national affairs adviser at BirdLife Australia, concerned that the spread of the virus has now reached a critical new stage.

“When people think of a seagull, they’re almost always thinking of the silver gull,” said Dooley.

“They’re very common, and primarily they are coastal, but they do come inland and can turn up in Lake Eyre following floods,” said Dooley.

Silver gulls are the second Australian native species to catch the disease, after dozens of detections in greater crested terns.

But it is the silver gull’s behaviour and habits that have experts concerned because they scavenge from dead or dying animals, meaning they can easily pick up the disease from other sick birds.

They also pick detritus from water bodies – lakes and flooded areas included – and these are known to be breeding grounds for the disease.

“There is such a large population of silver gulls, and they move into other habitats. They could be the vector that takes bird flu inland,” says Dooley. “They’re also really successful in urban areas and could bring the disease into those bird populations.”

Because Australia has a high concentration of unique birds, the susceptibility of many native species isn’t known. But the fears are there is no reason to think they would manage any better than birds overseas.

Birds that flock around water have tended to be the hardest hit. Examples include sandwich terns, black-headed gulls and northern gannets in Europe and, in Peru, pelicans.

Dooley said the mood at BirdLife Australia this week had been one of “trying to suppress that sinking, gut-churning feeling”.

The winter season for birdwatchers along the coast had been one of the best in 10 years, said Dooley, with rare petrels turning up in numbers along the east coast.

“Now that has been heavily tinged because probably among those were birds carrying H5N1.”

australia.title: Petrol prices on track to top $2 a litre as Bowen sounds death knell for fuel excise relief
australia.snippet: Petrol now costs more than $1.90 a litre in every capital city, with diesel expected to exceed $2.40 a litre Get our breaking news email ...
australia.content:
Petrol prices could surpass $2 a litre and diesel $2.40 in coming days, after the government’s 16-cent discount ends on Sunday.

The 32-cent per litre reduction in fuel excise, introduced in March at the peak of the fuel price spike, was halved to 16 cents in July.

The excise will return to its normal level on 3 August, adding 16 cents per litre to the wholesale prices paid by service stations.

Chris Bowen, the energy minister, told reporters on Saturday the government would not extend the temporary cost-of-living relief.

“Obviously we always monitor the situation and take steps as necessary, but our policy decision is clear,” Bowen said.

A 16 cent increase in fuel prices would add $8.80 to the cost of filling up, for a vehicle with a 55-litre tank.

Tom Woodlock, a senior market analyst at Argus Media, said service stations typically took four or more days to adjust prices at the pump to match changes in excise or overseas pricing.

Retailers have already passed higher wholesale fuel prices on to customers after the US resumed strikes on Iran in mid-July, pushing up oil and import costs.

Unleaded petrol prices have risen to 205.6 cents per litre in Canberra, 204.4 in Darwin and 200.5 in Hobart, according to MotorMouth data on Saturday.

Petrol costs more than 190 cents in every capital city, meaning it would pass 200 cents if the 16-cent increase was passed on in full.

Melbourne was facing diesel prices of 242.7 cents per litre on Saturday, up 68 cents from its June low of 173.9 cents, according to Motormouth. Canberra was at 244.4 cents a litre, Darwin at 244.1 and Hobart 241.8.

Diesel costs more than 235 cents per litre in every capital city except Perth, meaning it would pass 250 cents if service stations pass on the price hike in full.

The strait of Hormuz has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago. Iran struck two tankers under US escort on Friday after the two countries resumed trading strikes this week.

Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, has risen from about US$70 on 2 July to nearly US$90 on Saturday, pushing up import prices in Australia’s region.

Some analysts have predicted oil prices will return to US$100 a barrel if conflict continues. In March, when oil hit that price, and Australia had no fuel excise relief, petrol surpassed 250 cents a litre, and diesel passed 300 cents.

Economists have credited the excise discount with suppressing Australia’s inflation rate and supporting household spending as the economy weakens. Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said in a note on Saturday the loss of the discount could push petrol prices up to 210 cents a litre.

“This will push up headline inflation again as well as the cost of the average household’s weekly fuel bill by around $20,” Oliver said.

Bowen on Saturday defended the decision to end the discount and the related heavy vehicle road user charge, paid by trucks. He warned against panic buying and repeated the government’s call for motorists to buy only the amount of fuel that they need.

“I think Australians have understood … this is a temporary measure,” he said.

Bowen said Australia had 43 days’ worth of petrol stocks, 39 days of diesel, and 34 days of jet fuel. As of Saturday, 44 fuel ships were on the way to Australia with 3.1bn litres set to be delivered in the coming month, consistent with previous weeks, he said.

Fuel orders were locked in through up to October, and no orders to Australia had been cancelled during the international crisis, Bowen said.

australia.title: Adani to pay no company tax despite $1bn revenue from Queensland coalmine
australia.snippet: Indian conglomerate offsets earnings from Carmichael mine to report $340.6m loss, after promising billions in taxes and royalties Get our...
australia.content:
Indian conglomerate Adani will pay no company tax despite generating almost $1bn in revenue from coal mining in Queensland over the past year.

Financial accounts show the Carmichael thermal coal operations used large costs – including production and related party logistics expenses – to offset its $963.5m revenue in the 12 months to 31 March. This resulted in a recorded $340.6m loss for the year, erasing its tax bill.

Guardian Australia analysis of company accounts shows the mining project has never paid corporate tax after opening in 2021, despite past pledges by Adani that the operations would plough billions of dollars in taxes and royalties into the economy.

Adani Mining’s accounts show that it paid $58m in royalties in the 12-month period. Royalties are payments made to governments to extract state-owned minerals. Adani also paid a $33.1m royalty to a related party.

Tim Buckley, a former investment banker and the director of Climate Energy Finance, said the company was structured so that it wouldn’t pay corporate tax in Australia.

“This is a perfect example of why Australia needs new rules that ensure foreign entities have a sensible capital structure,” said Buckley, who advocates for changes that would limit the amount of deductions a business can make to reduce tax.

Adani’s project approval in central Queensland’s Galilee Basin was fiercely contested, opening a new jurisdiction of thermal coal extraction that raised environmental concerns.

Industry groups supporting the conglomerate had claimed Adani’s project would fund schools, hospitals and other infrastructure for “almost a century” through mining taxes and royalties.

A spokesperson for Adani Mining said the project provided direct jobs for more than 1,400 Queenslanders last financial year.

“We comply fully with our state and commonwealth taxation and royalty obligations and our statutory profit and tax outcomes are determined in accordance with Australian accounting standards and the corporations act,” the spokesperson said.

The Carmichael operations opened during a prosperous time for coalminers. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sent global energy prices soaring in 2022. Coal prices are now also being supported by energy supply constraints caused by conflict in the Middle East.

The Adani-controlled Abbot Point port business, named North Queensland Export Terminal, also did not pay any company tax over the most recent 12-month reporting period, despite earning $356.6m.

Various operating expenses lead to a $6.8m loss, with no tax payable.

The terminal business’s chief executive, Mark Smith, said accounts were prepared in accordance with Australian accounting standards and reflect the capital-intensive nature of owning and operating major export infrastructure.

“The terminal plays an important role in supporting Queensland trade and we remain focused on delivering safe, reliable, and efficient export services for our customers,” Smith said.

australia.title: Missing Australian hiker found dead in Wyoming, officials say
australia.snippet: Body of William Standish discovered in Teton mountains as investigators say fatal fall likely cause of death A 28-year-old Australian hik...
australia.content:
A 28-year-old Australian hiker who lost contact with his family while hiking the Continental Divide Trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks in Wyoming has been found dead, according to authorities.

The man, identified as William Standish, was discovered by rescuers on Wednesday morning in the Wigwams, a series of rocky peaks on the west slope of the Teton mountain range, the Teton county coroner said. Investigators say it was likely he suffered a fatal fall.

Standish had been attempting a thru-hike of the Continental Divide Trail between the Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks when he disappeared after contacting his family on 23 July, according to a statement from Teton county rescuers.

Evidence suggests Standish may have fallen from a steep ridgeline that separates Grand Teton and the Jedediah Smith wilderness, officials said.

Standish was discovered by a helicopter team after it spotted an orange backpack – and then saw his remains below the ridge.

His family said it had stopped receiving updates from him via a Garmin GPS device and Facebook Messenger on 23 July, leading to a search being mounted by Teton county rescue crews.

On 19 July, Standish gave an update from a location near Old Faithful, and described his planned route in the Tetons, Gros Ventre wilderness, the Wind River range, and the Divide Basin.

Four days later, the family received a Garmin check-in without coordinates or a message. There was also a Facebook Messenger video that they believe placed him in the Wigwams.

The Teton county search and rescue team said it “sends its sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased”. It also expressed gratitude to federal agencies who assisted in searching for Standish.

Standish had reportedly been following a popular thru-hike, or end-to-end through-hike, starting in Canada, the most northern point of the 3,100-mile Continental Divide Trail – which passes down through Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico.

There have been other hiking-related deaths in North America recently.

The Colorado Sun reported that a 15-year-old boy died after being struck by lightning on the state’s Mount Blue Sky on Monday. Sheriff’s officials identified the boy as Levi Strobel. Four other people were seriously injured, including Levi’s younger brother.

In Arizona, a man died during a hike on Phoenix’s South Mountain. Richard Fletcher, 61, left his home early on Saturday morning. Investigators later said his death was consistent with a heat-related or medical event, authorities told local media.

A 62-year-old man died in New Hampshire when he suffered a medical emergency in the state’s Welch-Dickey trail in the White Mountains. He was evacuated by national guard helicopter and later pronounced dead, according to New Hampshire Public Radio.

Two hikers also died in Canada’s Banff national park. One was a woman in her 20s after falling from a mountain near Marvel Peak on Tuesday. Three days earlier, a 65-year-old from Calgary fell from Mount Temple, also in Banff, the CBC reported.

world.title: Spanish PM calls for urgent EU meeting after ‘selfish’ responses to Ceuta crisis
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez hits out at ‘polarising and unlawful reaction’ over mass crossing into Spanish enclave in north Africa Europe live – latest...
world.content:
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has called for an urgent meeting of EU interior ministers after what he called some member states’ “selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction” to this week’s mass border crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, in north Africa.

More than 50,000 people crossed into the territory from Morocco on Thursday and Friday, with at least 67 people dying in the attempt. Some drowned, while others were crushed as they tried to cross a breakwater barrier.

Although more than 48,000 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday, the influx triggered a political crisis for the Madrid government and led some fellow EU countries to call for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

Italy announced on Friday evening that it would suspend its Schengen arrangements with Spain, even though Ceuta – and Spain’s other north African enclave, Melilla – are subject to special Schengen rules that prevent onward movement within the zone.

Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now-closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.

Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”.

Sánchez was equally forthright in a letter sent to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Council president, António Costa, and Micheál Martin, the prime minister of Ireland, which holds the EU presidency.

In the letter, the Spanish prime minister said he had been deeply concerned by the reaction some EU governments had shown to events in Ceuta.

Sánchez said that while most had expressed support and solidarity, others had chosen to attack Spain and call for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen area.

“Such an attitude – driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest – is … contrary to European law, humanitarian law, and the principles of solidarity that bind us together,” he said.

In a pointed rebuke to Italy, he noted that Spain was “according to Frontex, one of the least porous external borders of the European Union, with a number of irregular entries that is half that recorded, for example, in Italy in recent years (2021–2026)”.

He concluded by saying the EU could not afford “this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction” and asked for an urgent video conference of EU interior ministers to address the issue.

Senior EU officials are due to meet on Saturday in a “political crisis response team” convened by Ireland’s presidency. The meeting is designed to help member states make clear responses using expert opinion.

Ireland’s justice minister, Jim O’Callaghan, who is leading the meeting on behalf of the EU, said he had been in touch with Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, to express his solidarity and support.

“I will remain in close contact with the Spanish government, member states and the EU institutions as the situation evolves,” he said on Friday night.

Many of the remaining people who crossed into Ceuta returned to Morocco on Saturday morning amid a reinforced Spanish police and military presence.

“We hope to go to Europe to work and earn a living – that’s it,” Souleil Boyan, a 19-year-old from Senegal, told Agence France-Presse outside a migrant centre in Ceuta where dozens of other people from sub-Saharan Africa were waiting for officials.

“We all know that in Africa there isn’t much opportunity,” he added.

The Spanish government said in a statement that the situation in Ceuta remained calm and quiet.

“Friday night passed without incident,” it said. “Entries were completely halted, while departures to Morocco continued without any notable events.”

It said containment barriers were being installed at the Tarajal beach breakwater, including a 500-metre-long inflatable barrier and a line of anchored buoys.

world.title: At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident At least 57 people have d...
world.content:
At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.

The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a mixed reaction from other EU countries, including calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

Sánchez, who arrived in Ceuta on Friday morning, said he would use all the resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the city’s population.

He attributed the mass crossing to “human trafficking mafias” that had taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta, or Spain’s other north African enclave of Melilla, could not be summarily returned under special rules.

Sánchez said: “That has spread like wildfire during these last few hours through the networks of mafias that traffic in human beings and has produced an avalanche of the characteristics and dimension that we experienced yesterday.”

Sánchez said a temporary reception centre would be established to facilitate the documentation, registration, triage and “expedited” expulsion of people with no legal claim to be in Spain.

He also said the government would erect a visible barrier – a line of buoys – near the breakwater at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach to make it clear where the border was, and to legally comply with the court’s ruling.

Although the Spanish government said about 50,000 people had crossed the border on Thursday and in the early hours of Friday, the president of Ceuta put the figure at about 60,000.

Spain’s interior ministry, which has deployed additional police officers and soldiers to the enclave, said more than 48,300 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday.

The Irish presidency of the EU has convened a meeting of member states on Saturday, under the Integrated Political Crisis Response mechanism.

EU sources said this will provide experts from member states with an opportunity “to discuss the movements into Ceuta over the last two days, the numbers of people who have returned to Morocco today, the supports being provided by the EU to Spain and diplomatic engagement with Morocco”.

A further meeting of EU ambassadors has been called in Brussels on Monday.

The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over the course of two days.

That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.

That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group.

Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.

Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.

Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich, was quoted by the Associated Press as saying that “we have always prioritized legal, orderly and safe migration for all” and indicated that the situation had developed against Rabat’s wishes.

Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing officers of the Spanish Guardia Civil – which patrols Spain’s borders – described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”.

Without shelter, thousands of people, including unaccompanied children, had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements, while others roamed the streets aimlessly. “It’s chaotic,” said Sbihi.

Among those who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said.

Video footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children.

Ceuta and Melilla have the E​U’s only land border with ​Africa. ‌Both cities ​periodically ​experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reach Europe.

The events in Ceuta led some EU countries to issue strong threats or rebukes.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.

Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”.

Italy announced on Friday evening that it would be suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain, but the practical impact of the move was not immediately clear.

Meloni said the measure would be kept in force only as long as needed, adding: “In parallel, Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.”

Responding to Italy’s unilateral decision, a European Commission spokesperson said a member state “may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security”. But they added that the member state would need to notify the commission and explain how the situation in Ceuta constituted such a threat.

The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of its EU partners of its decision.

The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, urged Spain to “act swiftly to regain control of the situation and fulfil its commitments within Schengen cooperation”.

The Finnish interior minister, Mari Rantanen, said that as Spain had “completely failed to protect the Schengen area’s external border”, all EU countries should support Italy’s proposal to suspend its Schengen status.

However, in a statement later on Friday, the European Commission said Ceuta and Melilla were subject to special Schengen rules that prevented onward movement within the zone.

The EU’s migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, called the situation in Ceuta “unacceptable” and said he was in close contact with the Spanish authorities. But he also confirmed there was no onward route from Ceuta given the enclave’s unique status under the Schengen rules.

He said: “The Schengen borders code provides for special rules that apply to Ceuta and Melilla. Border checks on persons departing from Ceuta and Melilla remain in force.”

But there were also shows of unity. The European Council president, António Costa, expressed his “solidarity with Spain in the current situation of illegal migration in Ceuta”.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and to offer assistance to Spain. But, as a precautionary measure, Macron said he had asked the interior ministry to strengthen the French controls on its border with Spain with four mobile units and drones.

In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) called on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient.

In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.” The far-right Vox party called the incident “an invasion”.

On Friday evening, hundreds attended an anti-migrant rally outside the Moroccan embassy in Madrid, with images showing some protesters performing Nazi salutes and waving flags with far-right insignia.

world.title: Archbishop of Canterbury vows to support £100m pledge helping communities affected by enslavement
world.snippet: During visit to Ghana, Sarah Mullally expresses regret and says controversial fund symbolises Christian belief in repentance At a former ...
world.content:
At a former British castle where thousands of enslaved Africans were held before being shipped across the Atlantic, the archbishop of Canterbury expressed “lament” for the Church of England’s involvement in transatlantic chattel slavery and reaffirmed her commitment to a controversial £100m fund for affected communities.

Sarah Mullally made the comments during a visit to the Cape Coast castle, a 17th-century fortress built by Swedish traders, but occupied by the Danish and the Dutch, before the British seized it in 1664.

It was part of a 10-day tour of Ghana and Cameroon at the invitation of the head of the Anglican church’s west Africa province, the archbishop Cyril Kobina Ben-Smith.

“Being at Cape Coast castle today and seeing the horrific conditions that thousands of people were kept in, it is impossible not to feel the weight of the immense evil that drove the transatlantic slave trade,” Mullally said on Thursday.

She was shown the dungeons used to keep enslaved people, before praying in a former Anglican chapel above them. She also visited the “Door of No Return”, where enslaved people were loaded on to ships and ferried across the Atlantic. It has since been renamed the “Door of Return”.

Her trip began in the Ghanaian capital of Accra, about 90 miles (145km) east of Cape Coast on Sunday. There, Mullally visited four local parishes and delivered the sermon at a special Eucharistic service at St Joseph the Worker Anglican church in the Kaneshie area. According to local reports, the service was officiated by an all-female clergy from the Anglican church of Ghana.

Mullally, who in March became the 106th head of the 492-year-old denomination and the only woman to do so, also met the Ghanaian president, John Mahama, earlier in the tour, along with her husband, Eamonn Mullally.

Since the government launched the Year of Return scheme in 2019 to help Africans and their descendants in the diaspora reconnect with their roots, Ghana has had a surge in visitors. As part of Mullally’s visit, she laid a foundation stone for a hostel belonging to the local church’s culture resort initiative, to accommodate pilgrims from the diaspora wanting to engage in the scheme.

The archbishop also preached at a service of more than 1,000 nurses in the town of Mampong, where she commissioned a new campus clinic named after her. On Friday, she was heading to Yaoundé, the Cameroonian capital, and will then proceed to Douala and the English-speaking cities of Buea and Limbe.

Ghana has been spearheading a global campaign to seek reparative justice and last month hosted a landmark conference attended by more than 80 heads of state.

The archbishop’s visit comes three years after her predecessor Justin Welby formally apologised for the church’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, including using a fund for poor clergy to invest in enslaving Africans. “It is a stain on the wider church that some Christians did not see their brothers and sisters as created in the image of God, but as objects to be exploited,” he said.

The church set up a £100m fund committed to “a programme of investment, research and engagement” in communities affected by slavery, prompting diverse reactions. At the time, an independent oversight group argued that the amount was insufficient to address the generational damage slavery had caused and urged the church to expand that commitment to £1bn. Upon Mullally’s ascension to the role of archbishop, a committee of Conservative MPs urged her to spend the money on wages for the church’s clergy.

However, on Thursday, the archbishop reaffirmed her commitment to the fund. “We played a part in the transatlantic slave trade … part of the Christian belief in repentance is about action, so we are putting in place action to support those communities that feel the legacy of the slave trade,” she said.

Across Ghana, the mood has largely been celebratory. On a visit to the palace of the Asantehene, the traditional ruler of the Asante people, in the city of Kumasi on Wednesday, Mullally wore a special cassock and cape lined with kente cloth that pleased palace chiefs.

Among the less enthused was Accra-based accountant Kenneth Mordzro, who said he believes the church can play a greater role in reparation efforts. “They should bring back the gold and artefacts they stole from our ancestors during the colonial days,” he said, referring to items looted by the British government during the Anglo-Asante wars of the 19th century.

world.title: Ebola outbreak in DRC the fastest growing in the history of the virus
world.snippet: As the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers f...
world.content:
The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has made this latest outbreak the fastest growing in the known history of the virus.

At 3,360 confirmed cases, the disease is now affecting people in five provinces in the east of the DRC, with 1,487 deaths recorded, representing an overall case fatality rate estimated at about 45%, according to Congolese health officials. Health responses to the outbreak have been badly hampered by conflict in many of the affected areas.

“I fear that at some point, life may come to a standstill here in our province of Ituri,” said Deborah Nzuva, a mother of four who lives in Rwampara, one of the affected regions. “We were already in a precarious situation before the Ebola virus disease, which continues to claim its victims.”

Since officially declared by the Congolese authorities on 15 May, the Bundibugyo strain of the virus has spread faster than any of the country’s 16 previous Ebola outbreaks – and the numbers are approaching the previous worst toll, in 2018-2020 when 3,470 people in DRC were infected.

Prof Pierre Akilimali, from the country’s public health institute (NPHI), is in charge of the Ebola response. He emphasises that the disease continues to spread and that it is still difficult to know when it will reach its peak. According to him, there is a way to go and the road to bringing the outbreak under control is a long one.

“Here in Ituri, we have the issues of insecurity, mining and high population density, which make the current outbreak more complex than previous ones,” he said.

The Congolese authorities say they have taken a number of measures to limit spread, including strengthening surveillance through community liaison officers, building more than 20 Ebola treatment centres, and setting up local laboratories for testing. “The public must also play their part by seeking medical advice at the slightest suspicion of infection,” Akilimali said. “This will help us to respond effectively to the disease.”

He said cases continue to rise in the Bunia and Rwampara health zones, with between 100 and 150 new confirmed infections each week.

Annabelle Nissi, a clothing trader in Bunia, said people were living in fear.

“This outbreak is causing us great distress. Our hope lies solely in God’s hands. It continues to disrupt our lives and has brought our development projects to a standstill,” she said.

Dr Justus Nsio, field incident manager for the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said it was a race against time.

“All the experts monitoring this outbreak agree that it was detected too late. When detection is delayed, we have to work hard to make up for what we missed earlier in order to contain the disease,” he said.

“What is certain is that, with the commitment of the movement and our partners, the outcome will be favourable.”

Clinical trials began in early July of a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no standard treatment.

As of 15 July, about 20 people had been enrolled in these trials, which could last up to four months, according to Prof Placide Mbala, head of laboratory operations for the Ebola response in the DRC.

Uganda, which this week declared the Ebola outbreak over on its territory, 12 days after its last case was reported, has sent experts to the DRC to work alongside their Congolese counterparts, particularly in the border regions of Tchomia and Kasenyi.

world.title: US government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conference
world.snippet: State department ‘takes full responsibility’ for erroneous, widely shared chart displayed at Aids conference in Brazil A US government ma...
world.content:
A US government map of Africa mislabeled every country during a state department presentation at a ⁠global conference in Brazil ⁠this week, ​causing a stir among attenders who took screenshots and posted them online.

Reuters viewed a video of the presentation given at the Aids 2026 conference in ⁠Rio de Janeiro, which shows the errant map displayed halfway during a presentation about the state department’s new health agreements.

A Reuters analysis found the image of the map included ⁠in the presentation contained an artificial intelligence watermark that signals it was made with OpenAI tools. The ​company said it was investigating the report.

The state ‌department said it took “full responsibility” ‌for the confusion caused and that the map had been produced by a team member who hastily changed ‌the slide deck before the event.

The map showed Nigeria, where the US currently has several hundred troops deployed, as landlocked in the Sahara desert. Mozambique, which is in south-eastern Africa, was relocated to the Horn of Africa, while Côte d’Ivoire in west Africa was placed on the other side of the continent.

Screenshots of the map first appeared in a Substack post by the Aids expert Emily Bass and were widely ‌shared on LinkedIn, with one post garnering about 40,000 views.

“Whoever created and approved this slide did not know where countries in Africa are and did not care to ​check their work,” wrote Matt Petit, who focuses on AI and geopolitics at the Atlantic Council, in the post.

In a statement, the state department said: “We take full responsibility for the confusion and misrepresentation it caused for attendees, including our African partners.” The speaker at the conference was Jeff Graham, the ⁠top US health envoy who oversees the initiative known as the President’s Emergency Plan ​for Aids Relief, or Pepfar. He ​did not reply to requests for comment.

The ​state department said the discussions at the conference were “substantive and constructive” despite the map ​and that it remained ‌committed to fighting Aids ​with real results. The ​Trump administration’s decision last year to pause funding pending a review disrupted aid programs worldwide, but Pepfar’s core work such as the provision of life-saving drugs has largely resumed. The US is scaling back other areas of its spending including on prevention and surveillance, and plans to fully phase out the program in South Africa.
